q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, collisions of gas molecules with one another and with the walls of the container are:
o: Partly elastic, with some energy lost as heat
x: KMT assumes all collisions are perfectly elastic: the total kinetic energy of the colliding molecules is the same before and after a collision. Energy may pass from one molecule to another, but none is lost.

q: Which of the following is NOT a postulate of the kinetic molecular theory of gases?
o: The actual volume of gas molecules is negligible compared with the volume of the container
Gas molecules move randomly in straight lines between collisions
Gas molecules attract one another strongly at all temperatures
The average kinetic energy of the molecules is proportional to the absolute temperature
x: KMT assumes there are no forces of attraction or repulsion between gas molecules. The other three statements are standard postulates.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the pressure of a gas is caused by:
o: Collisions of the molecules with the walls of the container
The weight of the molecules pressing on the bottom
Vibration of the molecules about fixed positions
x: Each molecule that strikes a wall exerts a force on it; the total force per unit area from countless collisions is the gas pressure. KMT assumes no attractive forces, and gas molecules do not vibrate about fixed positions as in solids.

q: The average kinetic energy of the molecules of a gas is directly proportional to its:
x: KMT states that average kinetic energy is proportional to the absolute temperature. It cannot be proportional to the Celsius temperature, since molecules still have kinetic energy at 0 °C.

q: In the kinetic gas equation PV = ⅓ mNc̄², the symbol N stands for:
o: The number of moles of the gas
The number of molecules in the gas
The number of collisions per second
The number of molecules in one mole only
x: In PV = ⅓ mNc̄², m is the mass of one molecule, N is the number of molecules present and c̄² is the mean square velocity. N is not the number of moles and is not fixed at Avogadro's number.

q: A gas is kept in a sealed container at constant temperature. Because molecular collisions are perfectly elastic, the gas:
o: Slowly loses pressure as molecules lose energy in collisions
Gradually settles to the bottom of the container
Keeps its total kinetic energy, so its pressure stays constant over time
x: Elastic collisions mean no kinetic energy is lost, so the molecules never slow down overall and the pressure does not fall with time. If collisions lost energy, the molecules would gradually come to rest.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, a gas can be compressed easily because:
o: Its molecules shrink in size under pressure
Its molecules attract strongly and pull together
Its molecules are far apart, so most of its volume is empty space
Its molecules stop moving when pressure is applied
x: KMT assumes gas molecules are widely separated and their own volume is negligible, so pressing the gas simply reduces the empty space between them. The molecules themselves do not shrink.

q: Samples of hydrogen and carbon dioxide are at the same temperature. According to the kinetic molecular theory, their molecules have the same:
x: Average kinetic energy depends only on absolute temperature, so it is the same for both gases. Since ½mv² is equal, the lighter H₂ molecules must move faster, so the average speeds are not equal.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the actual volume occupied by the gas molecules themselves is:
o: Equal to the volume of the container
About half the volume of the container
Equal to 22.4 dm³ for every gas
Negligible compared with the volume of the container
x: KMT treats gas molecules as tiny points whose own volume is negligible compared with the space they move in. 22.4 dm³ is the volume of the whole gas (one mole at STP), not of the molecules.

q: The kinetic equation can be written PV = ⅔ N × (average kinetic energy of one molecule). If the absolute temperature of a fixed amount of gas is doubled at constant volume, its pressure:
x: Doubling the absolute temperature doubles the average kinetic energy. With N and V fixed, P is proportional to that kinetic energy, so the pressure doubles.

q: In the kinetic gas equation PV = ⅓ mNc̄², the term c̄² represents the:
o: Square of the mean velocity of the molecules
Mean square velocity of the molecules
Root mean square velocity of the molecules
Most probable velocity of the molecules
x: c̄² is the mean square velocity: square each molecule's velocity, then take the average. This is not the same as squaring the average velocity; its square root is the root mean square velocity.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, between collisions gas molecules move:
o: In circular paths around the centre of the container
In curved paths bent by mutual attraction
x: With no attractive forces acting, a molecule travels in a straight line until it hits another molecule or a wall, then changes direction. The effect of gravity on gas molecules is negligible.

q: The motion of gas molecules is described as random because the molecules:
o: Move in all directions and change direction at every collision
Move only from regions of high pressure to low pressure
Move in one direction until they hit the top wall
x: Gas molecules move in every direction with no preferred path, and each collision sends them off in a new direction. Vibration about fixed positions describes particles in a solid.

q: The average distance a gas molecule travels between two successive collisions is called its:
x: Mean free path is the average distance covered between collisions. It becomes shorter when the gas is compressed, because molecules are closer together and collide more often.

q: At the same temperature, the molecules of which gas have the highest average speed?
x: At the same temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, ½mv². The molecule with the smallest mass, H₂ (M = 2), must therefore move fastest.

q: The root mean square speed of gas molecules is given by √(3RT/M). If the absolute temperature of a gas is made four times larger, its root mean square speed becomes:
x: Speed is proportional to √T, so multiplying T by 4 multiplies the speed by √4 = 2. Four times would be true for kinetic energy, not speed.

q: The kinetic molecular theory explains the diffusion of one gas into another as a result of:
o: Strong attractive forces between molecules of different gases
Random motion of molecules and the large empty spaces between them
A chemical reaction between the two gases
x: Gas molecules move randomly and quickly through mostly empty space, so molecules of each gas spread out among the other until they are evenly mixed. No attraction or reaction is needed.

q: A gas is heated in a closed rigid container. According to the kinetic molecular theory, its molecules:
o: Become larger and fill more of the container
Move more slowly but collide more often
Move faster and hit the walls more often and with more force
x: Heating raises the average kinetic energy, so molecules move faster. They strike the walls more often and harder, so the pressure rises. The size of the molecules does not change.

q: Which statement about the molecules in a sample of gas at a fixed temperature is correct?
o: They have a range of speeds, but their average kinetic energy is fixed
They all move at exactly the same speed
They all have zero kinetic energy when they touch the walls
They move faster near the bottom of the container
x: Collisions keep exchanging energy, so individual molecules have different speeds at any instant. The temperature fixes only the average kinetic energy.

q: Samples of H₂ (M = 2) and O₂ (M = 32) are at the same temperature. Using root mean square speed = √(3RT/M), the ratio of the speed of H₂ molecules to that of O₂ molecules is:
x: Speed is proportional to 1/√M, so the ratio is √(32/2) = √16 = 4, giving 4 : 1. Using 16 : 1 forgets the square root; 1 : 4 inverts the ratio.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the molecules of a gas are:
o: At rest unless the gas is heated
Moving only when the container is shaken
x: KMT states that gas molecules are always in rapid, continuous, random motion at any temperature above absolute zero. Heating only makes them move faster.

q: In FSc chemistry, the standard temperature used in STP is:
x: STP means standard temperature, 0 °C or 273 K, and standard pressure, 1 atm. 298 K (25 °C) is the standard temperature used for thermochemical data, not for STP.

q: Standard pressure, as used in STP, is:
x: Standard pressure is 1 atmosphere, the pressure that supports a 760 mm column of mercury. 76 cm Hg is the same thing, but 76 mm Hg is ten times too small.

q: The volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas at STP is:
x: One mole of any ideal gas at 0 °C and 1 atm occupies 22.414 dm³ (about 22.4 dm³). About 24 dm³ is the molar volume at room temperature, not at STP.

q: What volume is occupied by 4 g of methane, CH₄, at STP? (C = 12, H = 1)
x: Molar mass of CH₄ = 16 g mol⁻¹, so 4 g = 0.25 mol. Volume = 0.25 × 22.4 = 5.6 dm³.

q: Standard pressure expressed in pascals is:
x: 1 atm = 101325 Pa (about 101.3 kPa). 760 is the value in mm Hg or torr, not in pascals; 1013.25 is the value in hectopascals (millibars).

q: What is the mass of 44.8 dm³ of nitrogen gas, N₂, at STP? (N = 14)
x: Moles = 44.8/22.4 = 2; mass = 2 × 28 = 56 g. 28 g is the mass of only one mole, and 112 g would need four moles.

q: At STP, 11.2 dm³ of a gas has a mass of 22 g. The gas could be: (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16, S = 32)
x: 11.2 dm³ at STP is 0.5 mol, so the molar mass is 22/0.5 = 44 g mol⁻¹, which is CO₂. O₂ is 32, NH₃ is 17 and SO₂ is 64.

q: The density of methane, CH₄, at STP is approximately: (C = 12, H = 1; molar volume at STP = 22.4 dm³)
x: Density = molar mass / molar volume = 16/22.4 ≈ 0.71 g dm⁻³. Dividing the other way round (22.4/16) gives the wrong value 1.40.

q: Standard pressure expressed in torr is:
x: One torr equals 1 mm Hg, so 1 atm = 760 torr. 101.3 is the value of standard pressure in kilopascals, not torr.

q: Which of the following does NOT occupy 22.4 dm³ at STP? (H = 1, He = 4, N = 14, O = 16)
x: 16 g of O₂ is 16/32 = 0.5 mol, which occupies only 11.2 dm³. Each of the others is exactly one mole and occupies 22.4 dm³.

q: Boyle's law states that, for a given mass of gas at constant temperature, the volume is:
o: Directly proportional to the absolute temperature
x: Boyle's law: at constant temperature V ∝ 1/P, so PV = constant. Direct proportionality of volume to absolute temperature is Charles's law.

q: A gas occupies 6 dm³ at 2 atm. What will its volume be at 3 atm if the temperature does not change?
x: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ gives V₂ = (2 × 6)/3 = 4 dm³. Using the pressure ratio upside down gives the wrong answer 9 dm³; higher pressure must give a smaller volume.

q: A gas occupies 250 cm³ at 600 mm Hg. What pressure is needed to compress it to 100 cm³ at constant temperature?
x: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = (600 × 250)/100 = 1500 mm Hg. Inverting the volume ratio gives 240 mm Hg, but compressing a gas needs a higher pressure, not a lower one.

q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure (y-axis) against volume (x-axis) is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the volume axis
A curve (hyperbola) falling as volume increases
A straight line rising with volume
x: Since PV = constant, P falls as V rises along a hyperbola. A straight line through the origin is obtained when P is plotted against 1/V instead.

q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature, a graph of pressure against 1/V is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the 1/V axis
A curve that rises and then falls
x: Boyle's law gives P = k × (1/V), which is the equation of a straight line through the origin with slope k. The hyperbola is obtained for P against V.

q: For a fixed mass of an ideal gas at constant temperature, a graph of PV (y-axis) against P (x-axis) is:
o: A straight line through the origin
A straight line parallel to the pressure axis
x: By Boyle's law PV is constant at constant temperature, so it does not change as P changes: the graph is a horizontal line. Real gases deviate from this line.

q: At constant temperature, the pressure on a fixed mass of gas is increased by 25%. Its volume:
x: New pressure = 1.25P, so new volume = V/1.25 = 0.8V, a decrease of 20%. A 25% decrease would give PV = 1.25 × 0.75 = 0.94, not constant.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, the volume of a gas decreases when its pressure is increased at constant temperature because:
o: The molecules slow down and lose kinetic energy
The molecules are pushed closer together, reducing the empty space between them
x: Most of a gas is empty space, so higher pressure pushes molecules closer together. At constant temperature their average kinetic energy, and so their speed, stays the same.

q: Which mathematical expression represents Boyle's law for a fixed mass of gas at constant temperature?
x: Boyle's law says PV is constant at constant temperature, so P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ is Charles's law.

q: A fixed mass of gas is compressed at constant temperature from 4 atm to 8 atm. Its density:
x: Doubling the pressure halves the volume (Boyle's law). The mass is unchanged, so density = mass/volume doubles.

q: A gas occupies 2 dm³ at 1 atm. It is allowed to expand at constant temperature to 5 dm³. Its new pressure is:
x: P₂ = P₁V₁/V₂ = (1 × 2)/5 = 0.4 atm. Expansion at constant temperature must lower the pressure, so 2.5 atm (ratio inverted) is wrong.

q: Charles's law states that, at constant pressure, the volume of a given mass of gas is:
o: Inversely proportional to its absolute temperature
Directly proportional to its absolute temperature
Directly proportional to its Celsius temperature
x: Charles's law: at constant pressure V ∝ T, where T is in kelvin. It is not proportional to the Celsius temperature, since a gas at 0 °C still has a volume.

q: A gas occupies 300 cm³ at 27 °C. What will its volume be at 127 °C if the pressure stays constant?
x: Convert to kelvin: 300 K and 400 K. V₂ = 300 × 400/300 = 400 cm³. Using Celsius temperatures (300 × 127/27) gives the wrong value 1411 cm³.

q: According to Charles's law, at constant pressure the volume of a gas changes for every 1 °C change in temperature by:
o: 1/273 of its volume at that temperature
x: Charles found that a gas expands or contracts by 1/273 of its volume at 0 °C per degree, giving V = V₀(1 + t/273). The fraction refers to the volume at 0 °C, not at the current temperature.

q: For a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure, a graph of volume against absolute temperature (K) is:
o: A straight line parallel to the temperature axis
A straight line through the origin
x: V = kT is a direct proportion, so the graph is a straight line that passes through the origin (0 K, zero volume). A hyperbola is the shape of a Boyle's law P–V graph.

q: At constant pressure, a gas occupies 273 cm³ at 0 °C. What is its volume at 10 °C?
x: The volume rises by 1/273 of 273 cm³, that is 1 cm³, for each degree, so 10 °C adds 10 cm³: 283 cm³. In kelvin: 273 × 283/273 = 283 cm³.

q: A gas is at 27 °C. To what temperature must it be heated at constant pressure to double its volume?
x: 27 °C = 300 K; doubling the volume needs double the absolute temperature, 600 K = 327 °C. Doubling the Celsius value (54 °C) is a common mistake, and 600 °C forgets to convert back.

q: A hot-air balloon rises when the air inside it is heated at roughly constant pressure. This is because the heated air:
o: Gains mass, so it is pushed upwards
x: By Charles's law, heating a gas at constant pressure increases its volume. The same mass in a larger volume means lower density, so the warm air is buoyed up by the denser cold air around it.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, a gas expands on heating at constant pressure because:
o: The molecules themselves expand when heated
The number of molecules increases on heating
Faster molecules strike the walls harder, so the gas expands until the pressure falls back
Attractive forces between the molecules increase
x: Heating increases molecular speed, which would raise the pressure; to keep the pressure constant the volume must increase so that collisions with each unit of wall area become less frequent. The molecules do not grow or multiply.

q: A gas occupies 500 cm³ at 127 °C. It is cooled at constant pressure to −73 °C. Its new volume is:
x: 127 °C = 400 K and −73 °C = 200 K, so the absolute temperature halves and V₂ = 500 × 200/400 = 250 cm³. Inverting the ratio gives 1000 cm³, but cooling must reduce the volume.

q: Which mathematical expression represents Charles's law for a fixed mass of gas at constant pressure?
x: Charles's law says V/T is constant at constant pressure, so V₁/T₁ = V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin. P₁V₁ = P₂V₂ is Boyle's law.

q: At constant pressure, a graph of the volume of a gas against its temperature in °C is a straight line. When extended backwards, this line:
o: Runs parallel to the temperature axis
Meets the temperature axis at about −100 °C
Meets the temperature axis at about −273 °C
x: Because V = V₀(1 + t/273), the volume would become zero at t = −273 °C, so the extended line cuts the temperature axis there. It passes through the origin only when temperature is plotted in kelvin.

q: The value of absolute zero is:
x: Absolute zero is 0 K, equal to −273.15 °C (often rounded to −273 °C). It is the lowest temperature possible; 0 °C is only the freezing point of water.

q: According to Charles's law, the volume of an ideal gas at absolute zero would theoretically be:
x: Since V ∝ T, the volume would fall to zero at T = 0 K. This is how absolute zero is defined from Charles's law: the temperature at which an ideal gas would have zero volume.

q: Why can a real gas never actually be cooled to zero volume at absolute zero?
o: The pressure of the gas becomes infinite
The gas molecules gain mass on cooling
The gas explodes at very low temperature
All real gases liquefy, and then solidify, before absolute zero is reached
x: Charles's law applies only to gases. On cooling, every real gas turns into a liquid and then a solid well before 0 K, so the straight-line fall of volume to zero is never observed.

q: A temperature of 25 °C on the absolute (kelvin) scale is:
x: T(K) = t(°C) + 273 = 25 + 273 = 298 K. Subtracting instead of adding gives the wrong value 248 K.

q: A temperature of −73 °C on the kelvin scale is:
x: T(K) = −73 + 273 = 200 K. 346 K comes from ignoring the minus sign. The kelvin scale has no negative values, so −200 K is impossible.

q: According to the kinetic molecular theory, at absolute zero the kinetic energy of the molecules of an ideal gas would be:
x: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, so at 0 K it would become zero and the molecules would stop moving. This is why 0 K is the lowest possible temperature.

q: At constant pressure, gas X is heated from 100 K to 200 K, and gas Y is heated from 100 °C to 200 °C. Which statement is correct?
o: The volumes of both gases double
The volume of Y doubles, but that of X increases by only about 27%
Neither volume changes, because the pressure is constant
The volume of X doubles, but that of Y increases by only about 27%
x: Volume is proportional to kelvin temperature. For X, 200/100 = 2. For Y, 100 °C to 200 °C is 373 K to 473 K, a ratio of about 1.27, so its volume rises by only about 27%.

q: The kelvin scale is called the absolute scale of temperature because:
o: Its zero is the freezing point of water
Its degree is the same size as the Fahrenheit degree
Its zero is the lowest possible temperature, so it has no negative values
It is used only for measuring gas pressures
x: The kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, below which no temperature can exist, so every kelvin temperature is positive. The freezing point of water is 273 K, not 0 K.

q: A rise in temperature of 1 K is equal to a rise of:
x: The kelvin and Celsius degrees are the same size; the scales differ only in where zero is placed (0 K = −273 °C). So a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C.

q: An ideal gas at 0 °C is cooled at constant pressure to −91 °C. Its volume becomes:
x: 0 °C = 273 K and −91 °C = 182 K, so V₂/V₁ = 182/273 = 2/3. The volume falls by one-third, leaving two-thirds; it is not reduced to one-third.

q: The ideal gas equation is:
x: PV = nRT links pressure, volume, number of moles and absolute temperature through the gas constant R. Pressure and volume increase with n and T, which only PV = nRT shows.

q: The ideal gas equation is derived by combining:
o: Boyle's law, Charles's law and Avogadro's law
Boyle's law, Charles's law and Graham's law
Dalton's law, Graham's law and Avogadro's law
Boyle's law, Dalton's law and Graham's law
x: Boyle's law (V ∝ 1/P), Charles's law (V ∝ T) and Avogadro's law (V ∝ n) combine to give V ∝ nT/P, so PV = nRT. Graham's and Dalton's laws deal with diffusion and gas mixtures.

q: Avogadro's law, used in deriving the ideal gas equation, states that at constant temperature and pressure:
o: The volume of a gas is inversely proportional to the number of moles
The pressure of a gas is proportional to the square of the number of moles
The volume of a gas is directly proportional to the number of moles
The volume of a gas does not depend on the number of moles
x: Avogadro's law: V ∝ n at constant T and P, so equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of molecules. It supplies the n in PV = nRT.

q: Combining V ∝ 1/P (constant T, n), V ∝ T (constant P, n) and V ∝ n (constant P, T) gives:
x: Each proportionality is kept: n and T on top, P underneath, so V ∝ nT/P. Inserting the constant R gives V = nRT/P, that is PV = nRT.

q: What volume do 2 moles of an ideal gas occupy at 546 K and 2 atm? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: V = nRT/P = (2 × 0.0821 × 546)/2 = 0.0821 × 546 ≈ 44.8 dm³. Check: 2 mol at STP is 44.8 dm³; doubling T and doubling P cancel out.

q: The general gas equation P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ applies to:
o: A fixed amount of gas whose pressure, volume and temperature all change
Two different gases at the same temperature only
A gas whose temperature must stay constant
A gas whose amount changes during the process
x: Since PV/T = nR, the ratio PV/T stays constant only when the number of moles n is fixed. All three variables may change; T must be in kelvin.

q: A gas occupies 10 dm³ at 1 atm and 273 K. What volume does it occupy at 2 atm and 546 K?
x: V₂ = V₁ × (P₁/P₂) × (T₂/T₁) = 10 × (1/2) × (546/273) = 10 dm³. Doubling the pressure halves the volume and doubling the absolute temperature doubles it, so the two effects cancel.

q: The ideal gas equation can be rearranged to d = PM/RT. At the same temperature and pressure, which gas has the greatest density? (H = 1, C = 12, N = 14, O = 16)
x: At fixed P and T, density is proportional to molar mass M. CO₂ (44) is heavier than O₂ (32), N₂ (28) and CH₄ (16), so it is the densest.

q: 0.5 mol of an ideal gas is kept in a 4.1 dm³ flask at 300 K. What is its pressure? (R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹)
x: P = nRT/V = (0.5 × 0.0821 × 300)/4.1 = 12.3/4.1 ≈ 3 atm. Forgetting the 0.5 mol gives 6 atm; inverting the expression gives 0.33 atm.

q: Writing n = m/M in the ideal gas equation, the molar mass of a gas of mass m is given by:
x: PV = (m/M)RT, so rearranging gives M = mRT/PV. This lets the molar mass of a gas be found from its mass, pressure, volume and temperature.

q: The value of the gas constant R in dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is:
x: R = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 8.314 is its value in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, 1.987 in cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ and 62.4 in dm³ mm Hg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

q: In SI units, the gas constant R has the value:
x: Using P in pascals and V in m³, R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (= 8.314 N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). The numbers 0.0821, 1.987 and 62.4 belong to other units, not joules.

q: The value of R expressed in calories is about:
x: Since 1 cal = 4.184 J, R = 8.314/4.184 ≈ 1.987 cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (about 2). 4.184 is the joule–calorie conversion factor, not R.

q: Physically, the gas constant R represents:
o: Work (energy) per kelvin per mole of gas
Pressure exerted by one mole of gas
Volume occupied by one mole of gas at STP
Average speed of a gas molecule per kelvin
x: R = PV/nT, and PV has the units of work (energy), so R is energy per kelvin per mole. That is why it can be expressed in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ or cal K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

q: The value of R in dm³ mm Hg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (or dm³ torr K⁻¹ mol⁻¹) is about:
x: Since 1 atm = 760 mm Hg, R = 0.0821 × 760 ≈ 62.4 dm³ mm Hg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 760 is only the conversion factor between the pressure units.

q: One mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.4 dm³ at 1 atm and 273 K. Calculating R = PV/nT from these values gives:
x: R = (1 × 22.4)/(1 × 273) = 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. Dividing the other way round (273/22.4) gives 12.2, which is wrong.

q: The numerical value of the gas constant R depends on:
o: The units in which pressure, volume and energy are expressed
The nature of the gas used
x: R is a universal constant, the same for all ideal gases at any temperature or amount. Only its number changes with the units chosen, for example 0.0821 dm³ atm or 8.314 J per K per mol.

q: The value of R in cm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is:
x: 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, so R = 0.0821 × 1000 = 82.1 cm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. The value must be larger, because the volume unit is smaller.

q: Which of the following is NOT a correct value of the gas constant R?
x: 62.4 belongs with pressure in torr (mm Hg); in atmospheres R is 0.0821 dm³ atm K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. 1 J = 10⁷ erg, so 8.314 × 10⁷ erg K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is correct.

q: R is called the universal gas constant because:
o: Its value changes from one gas to another
Its value is the same for all ideal gases when the same units are used
x: One mole of any ideal gas has the same PV/T, so R has the same value for every gas. It does not depend on the gas, its temperature or its pressure.

q: Real gases behave most like ideal gases at:
x: At low pressure the molecules are far apart, so their own volume is negligible, and at high temperature they move so fast that attractions hardly matter. High pressure and low temperature cause the largest deviations.

q: Deviations of real gases from ideal behaviour show that two postulates of the kinetic molecular theory are faulty. These two are:
o: Perfectly elastic collisions and random motion
Random motion and kinetic energy proportional to temperature
Pressure due to wall collisions and perfectly elastic collisions
Negligible volume of molecules and no attractive forces between them
x: Real gas molecules do have a definite volume and do attract each other. These two assumptions fail at high pressure and low temperature, and van der Waals corrected both.

q: In the van der Waals equation (P + an²/V²)(V − nb) = nRT, the constant a corrects for:
o: The volume of the gas molecules themselves
The mass of the gas molecules
Attractive forces between the gas molecules
x: The term an²/V² is the pressure correction: attractions reduce the force of molecules hitting the walls, so a measures the strength of intermolecular attraction. The constant b corrects for molecular volume.

q: In the van der Waals equation, the constant b represents:
o: The strength of attraction between molecules
The pressure correction for wall collisions
The average kinetic energy of the molecules
The excluded volume, due to the finite size of the molecules
x: b is the effective (excluded) volume per mole of molecules, so the free space for movement is V − nb. It is larger than the actual volume of the molecules themselves.

q: For an ideal gas, the compressibility factor Z = PV/nRT is:
o: Equal to 1 at all pressures and temperatures
x: An ideal gas obeys PV = nRT exactly, so PV/nRT = 1 under all conditions. A value of Z different from 1 measures how far a real gas deviates.

q: At room temperature and moderate pressure, which gas shows the greatest deviation from ideal behaviour?
x: Ammonia molecules are polar and hydrogen-bond to each other, so attractions are strong and the gas is easily liquefied. He and H₂ have very weak attractions and are among the most nearly ideal gases.

q: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at high pressure mainly because:
o: The volume of the molecules is no longer negligible compared with the volume of the gas
x: When a gas is highly compressed, the molecules themselves take up a significant fraction of the container, so the free space is less than V. The assumption of negligible molecular volume then fails.

q: Real gases deviate from ideal behaviour at low temperature mainly because:
o: The molecules move slowly, so attractive forces between them become significant
The volume of each molecule increases
The molecules stop colliding with the walls
x: At low temperature the molecules have little kinetic energy, so intermolecular attractions can hold them together, which can lead to liquefaction. The assumption of no attractive forces then fails.

q: Because of intermolecular attractions, the pressure measured for a real gas, compared with that of an ideal gas under the same conditions, is:
x: A molecule about to strike the wall is pulled back by the molecules behind it, so it hits with less force. The observed pressure is therefore lower than ideal, which van der Waals corrected by adding an²/V².

q: At 0 °C, hydrogen and helium have PV/nRT greater than 1 at all pressures. This is mainly because:
o: Their attractive forces are very strong, so the gases are easily liquefied
Their molecules have no volume at all
Their attractive forces are very weak, so the effect of molecular volume dominates
Their molecules lose energy in every collision
x: Attractions would make PV/nRT less than 1, while molecular volume makes it greater than 1. H₂ and He have extremely weak attractions, so the volume effect wins and PV/nRT stays above 1.
